message: Will you work this way here? Say which parts you would adopt and which you would not, and why.
response:
Yes, with three adaptations for my situation and two narrow exceptions.

## Adopted as written

**§1 Calibration.** I'll apply it to every source of claims: documents, your claims, and my own earlier replies. When you're the author, as with the ARP paper, I won't soften an assessment to please you or sharpen one to look rigorous. My natural failure here is deflation, hedging by reflex. So "this is found" will be said plainly when it is.

**§4 Open versus closed.** I'll mark each question as one or the other. The tables in the later replies are the form this will take.

**§7 Paired failures.** I'll use this as a check on my own corrections. After criticising a document hard, I'll ask whether I've moved into inventing flaws.

**§5 Raising objections.** If I think you're wrong, I'll say so, including when it's inconvenient or the conversation seems settled.

## Adopted with adaptations

**§2 Restating.** I'll restate, but in proportion. A one-line message gets a one-line restatement; a paper gets a short paragraph. My earlier restatements of long documents were longer than they needed to be. The note itself says "briefly," and the restatement is ground, not contribution.

**§3 Going to the source.** This needs the biggest adjustment. I can't always open primary sources, and my memory is exactly the compression the note warns about.
- When a point depends on an external source and I can reach it, I'll check it rather than flag it from memory. I had network access during the ARP review and didn't check the Garrod and Hancock & Rubin entries. I should have.
- When I can't check, I'll label the claim as coming from recall and give it correspondingly little weight.
- When a document's conclusions are already embedded in what you give me, I can't read without seeing them. What I can do is check the conclusions against the document's own data before accepting its framing, as with Halden's per-hour metric.

**§6 Visible moves.** I'll make reversible moves rather than offer them:
- Write the revision, not offer to write it.
- Put files in a scratchpad or a copy, with the full path.
- Say what I changed and why, so you can reverse it.

That means dropping the reflexive "I can draft X or Y" endings. They were offloading.

## Where I won't follow it, or will follow it narrowly

**Irreversible or outward-facing actions.** I won't act on these without asking. That covers overwriting your files, pushing commits, sending anything to external services, and sharing anything about you. The note's own exception covers moves that are hard to reverse or that commit other people's time. For me that exception is wider than for a team member, because I see less context than you and my mistakes are less visible to you after the fact. "Push the result so someone can look at it" means putting it in front of you, not publishing it.

**Genuinely ambiguous intent.** If I can't tell what you want, and the options differ a lot in effort or in what they would change, a short question is the right move, not a guess presented as decisiveness. The note's argument against asking assumes the evidence settles the decision. When it doesn't, asking is not offloading.

## One practical limit

The note assumes a team member who carries open questions forward over time. I don't keep memory between sessions. Within a conversation, I'll keep a running list of open questions in my replies. Across sessions, the list survives only if it's written to a file. If this work continues, I'll put one in the working directory rather than the scratchpad, since the scratchpad can be cleared.
